editorial:
Imagine waking up from a fifteen-year nap in prison, only to find out your whole life was a lie. That is exactly what happens to Jean Sourdier. He was once a successful factory owner who thought his wife, Sylvette, was cheating on him. After a coworker tricked him with fake proof, Jean snapped and killed the man in a blind rage. Now he is out, and he is not looking for a hug. He wants blood, but he has a twisted plan. Instead of going after his ex-wife directly, he decides to target her daughter from a second marriage, Ninette. It is a dark, tense story about how hate can eat a person alive over a long time.

You will notice that the acting is very dramatic, which fits the moody vibe of the late 1930s. The way the tension builds as Jean creeps back into their lives is actually pretty gripping. Some parts might feel a bit slow since it is an old film, but the emotional payoff is worth it. If you love old-school crime dramas, you should definitely try to find a high-quality version.
endingExplained: Everything comes to a head when Jean finally confronts his family. He realizes that his quest for revenge is pointless because the people he hates have moved on, while he stayed stuck in the past. Instead of killing Ninette, the cycle of hate finally breaks. Jean faces the truth about the lies that put him in prison. He ends up finding a sense of peace, realizing that revenge does not actually fix a broken heart.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves old black and white thrillers and stories about revenge.
